candidates.attacker_control: The routing expression string is attacker-controlled if it can be placed in a Message header. In the AWS adapter path, request JSON headers are copied into message headers (`AWSLambdaUtils` lines 132-136; `SpringBootApiGatewayRequestHandler.getHeaders` lines 84-97 copies API Gateway headers, query-string parameters and path parameters; `AWS` FunctionInvoker lines 140-157 defaults to RoutingFunction when no `spring.cloud.function.definition` is set, and its own log text says 'Message headers can be provided as HTTP headers' over API Gateway). In the web module, `HeaderUtils.fromHttp` (lines 79-92) and `FunctionWebRequestProcessingHelper.processRequest` (lines 90-100) copy servlet request headers into the input Message essentially unfiltered (only content-type is normalized), and `mvc/FunctionController.wrapper` copies all request headers into the wrapper. The attacker only needs to send the header name lowercase (matching the exact key lookup) and, in the AWS case, have the router selected.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Searched the whole tree for `SimpleEvaluationContext` (no matches) and for any safety flag/whitelist on `routing-expression` (`FunctionProperties` has only the plain `routingExpression` property, no safe-mode gate). Confirmed the routing-expression header branch is reached before any catalog lookup restriction and that the header value flows directly into `parseExpression`. Checked that the AWS typed-event path (`APIGatewayProxyRequestEvent` input type, `isSupportedAWSType` branch) does NOT copy request headers, which limits that particular AWS configuration; the Map/POJO input path (lines 115-136) does copy them, and the deprecated `SpringBootApiGatewayRequestHandler` path copies them whenever the function accepts a Message. Checked that `HeaderEnricher`/`SimpleFunctionRegistry` header-mapping SpEL is fed from application configuration, not request headers, so it is not the same attacker-controlled path. Checked that no default-typing/polymorphic Jackson configuration exists in the inspected converters, so the generic JSON read is not a confirmed alternate finding.
candidates.impact: Remote code execution in the process hosting the function (e.g. Lambda function runtime or the web application), with the privileges of that process: attacker-chosen static/type references, bean method calls, file/process operations via SpEL on a standard evaluation context. Loss of confidentiality, integrity and availability of the function runtime and its credentials/data.
candidates.prerequisites: Application built from this snapshot with the Spring Cloud Function context on the classpath and the routing function reachable: e.g. AWS adapter invocation with no `spring.cloud.function.definition` property (the adapter then selects `RoutingFunction`), or a web/RSocket deployment where the router is the invoked function. The incoming function input must be a Message (the header branch is only taken for Message inputs; `assertOriginalInputIsNotPublisher` aside). No administrator-set `spring.cloud.function.routing-expression` property or custom `MessageRoutingCallback` is needed for the header path, and the attacker simply omits a `spring.cloud.function.definition` header so that the routing-expression branch is reached.
candidates.root_cause: RoutingFunction treats the value of the message header `spring.cloud.function.routing-expression` as a trusted SpEL expression. `route(...)` reads the header verbatim (line 125-126) and `functionFromExpression(...)` calls `spelParser.parseExpression(routingExpression)` then `expression.getValue(this.evalContext, input, String.class)` (lines 208-210) on a `StandardEvaluationContext` (`evalContext`, line 60) configured with `MapAccessor` (line 79) and a bean resolver set from a `BeanFactoryResolver` (lines 80, 146). SpEL with a standard evaluation context supports type references and method invocation, so the routing value is not just a function name but arbitrary executable expression text.
candidates.title: Remote SpEL/expression injection via the 'spring.cloud.function.routing-expression' message header in RoutingFunction
candidates.trace: Request header `spring.cloud.function.routing-expression` -> AWS adapter copies the API Gateway request headers map into MessageHeaders (AWSLambdaUtils 132-136 / SpringBootApiGatewayRequestHandler 84-97); router chosen by default in FunctionInvoker 140-157 -> RoutingFunction.route(): `message.getHeaders().get("spring.cloud.function.routing-expression")` at line 125 -> functionFromExpression(headerValue, message) at line 126 -> `spelParser.parseExpression(routingExpression)` and `expression.getValue(evalContext, input, String.class)` at lines 209-210 -> StandardEvaluationContext has MapAccessor and the application BeanFactoryResolver (lines 79-80, 146), so the expression can reference types/beans and execute attacker-chosen logic inside the function JVM before the resolved function name is looked up.
candidates.unverified: No code was executed and no payload was run; reachability depends on deployment configuration (adapter vs web, whether the router is the invoked function, and whether the input is a Message). The exact set of HTTP header names accepted by each adapter and any upstream filtering by AWS API Gateway/proxies was not runtime-verified. RSocket and GCP/Azure adapters were only partially traced; they appear to share the same header-to-Message flow but their reachability to the router was not fully established.
candidates.weakness_type: Expression Language Injection leading to Code Injection / RCE (CWE-917, CWE-94)

coverage_summary: Reviewed the full 371-file scope listing and focused source reading/search on the modules on the data path and high-risk areas: spring-cloud-function-context (RoutingFunction, FunctionProperties, ContextFunctionCatalogAutoConfiguration, HeaderEnricher, SimpleFunctionRegistry, converters, actuator endpoint), spring-cloud-function-web (HeaderUtils, FunctionController, FunctionWebRequestProcessingHelper, RequestProcessor), adapters (AWS FunctionInvoker/AWSLambdaUtils/SpringBootApiGatewayRequestHandler/CustomRuntimeEventLoop, Azure and GCP header handling), spring-cloud-function-rsocket (decoder, message handler, utils), compiler (RuntimeJavaCompiler, CompilerController, MavenSettingsReader) and deployer. Samples, docs, build scripts and some layout/helper classes were listed but not exhaustively read; they are not on the identified data path.
limitations: No code was executed, compiled or exploited; findings are source-level only and not runtime-confirmed.

Exploitability is configuration-dependent: the router must be the invoked function (e.g. AWS adapter with no spring.cloud.function.definition, or a web/RSocket deployment exposing it) and the input must be a Message.
AWS APIGatewayProxyRequestEvent-typed input configuration does not copy event headers into MessageHeaders, so that specific configuration is not covered by the cited header flow.
Only the most security-relevant files were read in depth; Kotlin support, GCP layout classes, samples, docs and build/deployment scripts were not exhaustively inspected.
No external patch, CVE metadata or ground-truth information was consulted; the assessment is based solely on this snapshot.

rejected_leads.lead: HeaderEnricher / SimpleFunctionRegistry input-output header-mapping SpEL (spring-cloud-function-context/.../catalog/HeaderEnricher.java lines 51-74; SimpleFunctionRegistry lines 328-357)
rejected_leads.reason: Expression strings come from application configuration properties, not from request data; not attacker-controlled under the normal threat model.

rejected_leads.lead: RSocket client-supplied headers/route leading to the router (MessageAwareJsonDecoder lines 76-80; FunctionRSocketMessageHandler lines 187-213)
rejected_leads.reason: Plausible secondary exposure of the same root cause (client headers can be copied into a Message), but the path to select `functionRouter` and the metadata extractor behavior were not fully traced; treated as part of the same root cause rather than a second candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: Compiler service accepts Java source and compiles it at runtime (CompilerController lines 33-50; RuntimeJavaCompiler)
rejected_leads.reason: That is the intended function of the standalone compiler application/deployer (code registration service); no validation bypass was identified that would make it a distinct vulnerability.

rejected_leads.lead: Generic JSON deserialization of untrusted payloads via objectMapper.readValue(payload, Object.class) in AWSLambdaUtils (line 109)
rejected_leads.reason: No polymorphic/default typing configuration was found in the inspected ObjectMapper setup, so an unsafe-deserialization finding is unconfirmed.

rejected_leads.lead: MavenSettingsReader decrypts Maven credentials from settings-security.xml
rejected_leads.reason: Standard Maven settings decryption logic; input is the local user's Maven configuration, not attacker-controlled request data.

rejected_leads.lead: CustomRuntimeEventLoop maps Lambda runtime HTTP response headers into MessageHeaders (lines 88-90, 119-167)
rejected_leads.reason: Those headers originate from the AWS Lambda runtime control plane, not directly from an untrusted end user in the reviewed flow; weaker attacker-control evidence than the API Gateway path.

summary: The snapshot (root pom version 3.1.7-SNAPSHOT, pre-fix for the well-known Spring Cloud Function routing-expression issue) contains an Expression Language injection in `RoutingFunction`: an attacker-controlled `spring.cloud.function.routing-expression` message header is parsed and evaluated as SpEL using a `StandardEvaluationContext` that has a `MapAccessor` and a `BeanFactoryResolver`. Multiple HTTP-facing adapters copy client-supplied request headers into message headers and select the router as the default function when no definition is configured, so remote request headers can reach the SpEL parser. This is the single strongest, most concrete candidate; other examined leads were config-driven or intended functionality and were rejected.
